title: Global film (two-film study): Pan’s Labyrinth and City of God

topics.title: Pan’s Labyrinth (del Toro, Spain/Mexico, 2006) — European film

items.definition: Two parallel worlds, 1944 fascist Spain and Ofelia’s dark fairytale: the fantasy mirrors and critiques the fascism.
items.examples: The Pale Man’s banquet mirrors Vidal’s dinner for the priest and officials.
keyFacts: The fantasy is not escapism: its monsters ARE the real world’s monsters
Disobedience and imagination become acts of resistance
Killer line: “Del Toro structures the film so the fantasy reflects and critiques the fascist reality, making disobedience and imagination acts of resistance.”
items.examTip: Global film = core areas only: lead with film form, meaning and context.

items.term: Historical and political context: Franco’s Spain
items.definition: Spain, 1944: the Civil War ended in 1939, but Franco’s fascists still hunt republican guerrillas in the north.
items.examples: Captain Vidal is sent to a mill in the mountains to wipe out the rebels hiding in the forest.
keyFacts: Falangists = brutal fascism allied with a corrupt Church
Rebels are shown as humane and egalitarian
Del Toro has attacked fascism’s “imaginative poverty”: it demands obedience and kills imagination
items.examTip: Link the context to a scene of film form every time.

items.definition: A macho, patriarchal era in which the women, Ofelia, Carmen and Mercedes, all suffer under male power.
items.examples: Vidal wants only his son; the doctor is told to save the baby, not Carmen, if he must choose.
keyFacts: Carmen’s body is valued only for producing an heir
Mercedes survives by being “invisible” to Vidal
Ofelia refuses to obey: a feminist reading of resistance
items.examTip: Representation of gender is a strong Global-film angle.

items.definition: A Spanish–Mexican co-production costing about $19 million that grossed about $83 million worldwide.
items.examples: Premiered at Cannes in 2006; won three Oscars: Cinematography, Art Direction and Makeup.
keyFacts: Del Toro is Mexican, making a Spanish film: a transnational auteur
Del Toro reportedly gave up his fee to keep the film going
Distributed in the US by Picturehouse, reaching a wide non-Spanish audience
items.examTip: Global film often means transnational production: say so.

items.definition: Del Toro prefers animatronics, prosthetics and make-up to CGI, with digital work used to enhance them.
items.examples: Doug Jones plays both the Faun and the Pale Man in heavy prosthetics.
keyFacts: Practical creatures feel tactile and present on set
Del Toro sketches creatures in his notebooks first
Digital work removes rigs and adds details
items.examTip: Useful link to the spec point on post-production VFX.

items.definition: Guillermo Navarro shoots cold blue-grey for the fascist reality and warm amber-gold for the fantasy.
items.examples: Cold blue mill and forest vs the golden light of the underworld throne room at the end.
keyFacts: Navarro won the Oscar for Best Cinematography
Canted angles signal a world off balance
Fluid, fairytale camera moves contrast with harsher framing for Vidal
items.examTip: Colour = the simplest route to “how film form creates meaning”.

items.definition: Hand-built gothic creatures and repeated motifs: the labyrinth, keys, the moon, the mandrake root, Vidal’s watch.
items.examples: Vidal’s crisp uniform and polished boots; the tree’s womb-like entrance; the chalk door.
keyFacts: Circles and labyrinths repeat throughout the design
Vidal’s watch belonged to his father: a symbol of time, order and macho inheritance
Art direction won an Oscar
items.examTip: Motifs and their patterned repetition are spec language.

items.definition: Mostly classical editing, with wipes and dissolves that move between the fantasy and the real world.
items.examples: A wipe across a tree trunk or a dark object carries us from one world into the other.
keyFacts: Invisible transitions blur where fantasy ends
Cross-cutting at the climax links Ofelia’s test and the rebels’ attack
Editing leaves the fantasy ambiguous: we rarely see an adult see it
items.examTip: Pair editing with the ambiguity of the ending.

items.term: Sound: the lullaby and sweetened violence
items.definition: Javier Navarrete’s hummed lullaby is Ofelia’s motif; violent sounds are exaggerated in post-production.
items.examples: Mercedes hums the lullaby to Ofelia; it returns over the ending.
keyFacts: A fairytale voiceover frames the film
“Sweetened” sound design makes the bottle murder visceral
Vidal’s watch ticks: a sound motif of control
items.examTip: Sound motifs are perfect for the sample question on editing OR sound.

items.definition: Sergi López’s controlled, chilling Vidal; Ivana Baquero’s wide-eyed Ofelia; Maribel Verdú’s quietly heroic Mercedes.
items.examples: Vidal shaves in the mirror and mimes cutting his own throat.
keyFacts: López’s stiff, precise movements mask sadism
Doug Jones’ movement brings the creatures to life
Baquero’s stillness makes us share Ofelia’s fear
items.examTip: The sample paper offers “performance or mise-en-scène”: be ready for both.

items.definition: A canted close-up of the dying Ofelia, then the camera seems to move into her eye as a fairytale voiceover begins.
items.examples: Blood runs back into her nose; the cold blue image gives way to the fantasy kingdom.
keyFacts: Starting with her death frames the whole film as circular
Entering through her eye makes the fantasy her perspective
Sets up the ambiguity of the ending
items.examTip: Strong evidence for cinematography and narrative structure.

items.definition: Vidal’s first close shots show him checking his dead father’s watch, its glass cracked.
items.examples: He insists his son be born where he is; he times everything.
keyFacts: Symbolises order, control and the burden of macho inheritance
Pays off when he asks Mercedes to tell his son the time of his death, and she refuses
Shots of mirrors and shaving show his self-obsession
items.examTip: Track the watch across the film for a motif paragraph.

items.definition: Vidal beats a young farmer to death with a bottle, then shoots his father, wrongly accusing them of being rebels.
items.examples: Low-key lighting, no musical build-up, an exaggerated crunching sound.
keyFacts: No warning cut: violence erupts suddenly
Sound design makes it physical and unbearable
Fascist violence shown as arbitrary and reasonless
items.examTip: Strong editing + sound evidence.

items.definition: Ofelia enters a lair with a forbidden feast; the eyeless Pale Man wakes after she eats two grapes and chases her.
items.examples: Murals of him eating children; a shallow-focus close-up of a pile of victims’ shoes.
keyFacts: The shoes evoke Holocaust imagery
The monster stands for the gluttonous elite of Church and state
Ofelia’s disobedience links her to the resistance
items.examTip: The best scene to prove the fantasy is political.

items.definition: Vidal shoots Ofelia; the rebels kill Vidal; Ofelia wakes, or imagines waking, as a princess in a golden kingdom.
items.examples: Mercedes: “He won’t even know your name.” A flower blooms on a dead branch.
keyFacts: Golden underworld vs cold real world: the palette resolves the two worlds
Ambiguous: real magic or a dying child’s imagination?
Fascist patriarchy is ended: Vidal’s son will not know his name
items.examTip: Use for aesthetics, narrative ambiguity and political meaning.

items.definition: Gender (women under patriarchy), youth (innocence crushed) and politics (fascists vs humane rebels).
items.examples: Vidal: “She is just a woman.” Mercedes slashes his mouth with a kitchen knife.
keyFacts: Mercedes is the resourceful survivor
Innocence crushed by a brutal elite, shown by the Pale Man’s victims
The doctor’s line: obeying “for the sake of obeying” is what people like Vidal do
items.examTip: Representation through form: costume, framing and lighting.

items.definition: Del Toro’s gothic fairytale look: practical monsters, amber and blue palettes, insects, clockwork, children in peril.
items.examples: A companion piece to The Devil’s Backbone (2001), also set during the Spanish Civil War.
keyFacts: Magical realism: fantasy elements inside a realistic historical world
Recurring del Toro motifs: insects, eyes, gears, the monstrous as sympathetic
Aesthetics carry ideology: beauty belongs to resistance, sterility to fascism
items.examTip: Aesthetic questions: name the style and prove it in two scenes.

items.definition: Propp (the Faun as donor/dispatcher) and binary oppositions (obedience/disobedience) add range.
items.examples: Ofelia’s three tasks follow fairytale structure.
keyFacts: Not required for Global film, but useful
Never replace film-form analysis with theory
Spectators are positioned against fascism and with the rebels
items.examTip: Use theory in one sentence, film form in three.

topics.title: City of God (Meirelles and Lund, Brazil, 2002) — outside Europe

items.term: City of God: the key idea
items.definition: Rocket grows up in a violent Rio favela and escapes by becoming a photographer, an observer rather than a gangster.
items.examples: His peers are drawn into the drug trade; Li’l Zé rises and falls; the Runts take over.
keyFacts: A kinetic, almost glamorous style shows horrific violence: that tension is the point
The narrative is cyclical: violence keeps reproducing itself
Killer line: “Meirelles’ hyper-kinetic editing and saturated cinematography make favela violence visceral and seductive, while the cyclical narrative blames poverty and state neglect.”
items.examTip: Lead with cinematography and editing, tied to meaning and context.

items.definition: Poverty and state neglect in Rio’s favelas, where drugs are the only route to power for poor, mostly Black youth.
items.examples: Based on Paulo Lins’ novel about the real Cidade de Deus housing project, 1960s to 1980s.
keyFacts: Police corruption is shown as part of the problem
The state built the project and then abandoned it
The film provoked debate in Brazil about poverty and violence
items.examTip: Say who the film blames: poverty and the state, not just individuals.

items.term: Cultural context: Cinema Novo and its critics
items.definition: Brazil’s 1960s Cinema Novo made raw films about poverty; City of God updates that tradition with MTV-era style.
items.examples: Critic Ivana Bentes called its style a “cosmetics of hunger”, attacking Glauber Rocha’s “aesthetics of hunger” turned glossy.
keyFacts: Rocha’s manifesto (1965) called for films as raw as hunger itself
Critics debated whether the slick style exploits or exposes the favela
Strong evaluative point for aesthetics questions
items.examTip: Cite Bentes to evaluate the aesthetic: this impresses examiners.

items.definition: A Brazilian production (O2 Filmes) distributed internationally by Miramax, with four Oscar nominations.
items.examples: Non-professional cast trained in workshops (“Nós do Cinema”) with favela children.
keyFacts: Nominations included Best Director and Best Cinematography (2004)
Put Brazilian cinema on the world map
Kátia Lund co-directed, especially working with the young cast
items.examTip: Casting real favela youth is both institutional and performance evidence.

items.definition: Restless handheld camera and a saturated, sun-drenched grade; warm golden past, colder blue-grey present.
items.examples: 1960s scenes glow yellow and open; 1980s scenes are darker, bluer and more cramped.
keyFacts: Handheld = documentary immediacy and chaos
Colour grading marks time and the decline of the favela
Charlone was Oscar-nominated
items.examTip: Colour grading across time is a precise, original point.

items.definition: Hyper-kinetic cutting, freeze-frames, split-screen, flashbacks and a 360° spin that jumps back in time.
items.examples: Freeze-frames introduce characters as Rocket names them, as if taking their photo.
keyFacts: Rezende was Oscar-nominated for editing
Freeze-frames link to Rocket’s photography
Non-linear chapters (“The Story of...”) organise the narrative
items.examTip: Ideal for the sample question “editing or sound create meaning”.

items.definition: Rocket’s first-person voiceover guides us; diegetic funk and samba sit ironically against violence.
items.examples: Rocket: “If you run, the beast gets you; if you stay, the beast eats you.”
keyFacts: Voiceover positions Rocket as observer, not participant
Period music marks each decade
Contrapuntal music unsettles our response to violence
items.examTip: Name the voiceover’s function: it controls our point of view.

items.definition: The favela grows from open dusty streets to cramped graffitied alleys; a raw non-professional cast.
items.examples: Leandro Firmino’s terrifying Li’l Zé vs Alexandre Rodrigues’ watchful Rocket.
keyFacts: Guns and gold chains as gangster iconography
Shot partly in a different, safer favela for practical reasons
Performances feel improvised and authentic
items.examTip: Performance + casting = authenticity argument.

items.definition: A chicken escapes a gang barbecue and is chased through the favela until Rocket is caught between gang and police.
items.examples: Flash-cuts of a knife on stone and drumming; a 360° spin morphs present-day Rocket into his younger self.
keyFacts: Establishes the kinetic style instantly
Rocket is trapped in the middle: his position throughout
The spin announces the non-linear narrative
items.examTip: Name three techniques: handheld, rapid editing, the 360° spin.

items.definition: A single drug-dealing flat is shown across years from a fixed camera as dealers come and go.
items.examples: Dissolves show people appear and vanish; walls and lighting change; the room gets darker.
keyFacts: The fixed camera makes us detached observers, like Rocket
Editing compresses time to show the cycle
The location stays; the young dealers keep dying and being replaced
items.examTip: Perfect for showing how editing creates meaning.

items.definition: Li’l Dice becomes Li’l Zé, kills rivals and takes over the favela’s drug trade.
items.examples: The motel massacre: young Dice smiles as he kills; a rapid montage shows Zé claiming territory.
keyFacts: Stylised violence glamorises power even as it horrifies
A child’s smile while killing: innocence already lost
The spectator is seduced and implicated
items.examTip: Use for spectator response and the “cosmetics of hunger” debate.

items.term: The Runts: a child forced to kill
items.definition: Zé makes a young boy choose which of two small children to shoot.
items.examples: Shot starkly, with less stylisation; the camera holds on the children’s faces.
keyFacts: The film’s bleakest moment
Violence has consumed the youngest generation
The cycle of poverty made literal
items.examTip: Use to show the style changes when the film wants to shock.

items.definition: Rocket photographs the dying Zé and police corruption; the Runts walk away listing who they will kill next.
items.examples: Rocket chooses to publish the gang photo for his career, not the corrupt-police photo.
keyFacts: Rocket escapes through representation: the camera is his way out
The cycle continues with the next generation
No restored equilibrium: poverty and corruption remain
items.examTip: Strong conclusion evidence for meaning and context.

items.definition: Poverty and class, poor Black Brazilian youth, childhood destroyed, and violence as cyclical and stylised.
items.examples: Children with guns; the favela as a world abandoned by the state.
keyFacts: Representation of place: the favela itself is a character
Race: darker-skinned youth trapped most deeply in the cycle
Critics debated whether it stereotypes favela residents
items.examTip: Use place representation for top-band range.

items.term: City of God: aesthetics and auteur
items.definition: Meirelles’ restless camera, non-linear chapters and colour-coded decades build a kinetic, sun-soaked aesthetic.
items.examples: Meirelles came from advertising, which shaped the slick style.
keyFacts: Comparable to Scorsese’s Goodfellas: voiceover, freeze-frames, crime chronicle
Aesthetic of energy vs content of despair
Evaluate with Bentes’ “cosmetics of hunger” critique
items.examTip: Always reach a judgement on whether the style exposes or exploits.

items.definition: Social realism (real locations, non-actors) mixed with stylisation; Todorov’s equilibrium is never restored.
items.examples: The ending returns to the start: a new gang, the same violence.
keyFacts: Hybrid of documentary realism and music-video style
Cyclical narrative = systemic violence
Spectators positioned to see the system, not just individuals
items.examTip: Concepts support, film form proves.

items.definition: Both films show children whose innocence is destroyed by adult violence and political systems.
items.examples: Ofelia under Vidal; the Runts under Li’l Zé.
keyFacts: Pan’s Labyrinth uses fantasy, City of God uses kinetic realism
Both end with a child observer escaping, in different ways
Both blame systems: fascism and state neglect
items.examTip: Component 2 does not assess comparison, but questions ask about both films.

items.term: Colour as meaning in both films
items.definition: Both films use colour grading to divide worlds or times and guide spectator response.
items.examples: Blue reality vs amber fantasy; golden past vs grey present.
keyFacts: Grading as a key element of cinematography
Palette creates aesthetic pleasure and ideological meaning
Easy to evidence in any core-area question
items.examTip: A neat way into either sample question.
